preview: Interview experience of Yashvi Mehta for an internship at Hilti, detailing the pre-placement talk, online assessment, technical round, and HR round.
content: Interview Experience Yashvi Mehta - TY BTech CE, 231071079 HTSI Interview Experience Location: Pune Stipend: 80,000 INR. Timeline- PPT 24th July 8.30 a.m. OA 24th July (Online) Interview 25th July - 9 a.m. onwards (Offline) Results announced at around 5 p.m. Hilti was the 3rd company to visit the campus after De Shaw and Goldman Sachs. Pre-Placement Talk On 19th July 2024, the link to apply for Hilti was circulated. The pre-placement talk was on 24th July at 8.30 in the morning in the college auditorium. The Pre-Placement Talk was quite interesting. They started off with the history of the company, work culture and global presence. This was followed by a detailed explanation of the company’s operations and the products it develops, with particular importance on the role of software within all of it. It concluded with a short Q & A session. It’s important to pay close attention to what’s discussed and note down key points, as this provides a clear understanding of the company and the kind of interns they are looking for. Also, it serves as an important point to strike a conversation with the interviewer or answer firm related questions. This demonstrates genuine interest and awareness. Online Assessment Around 170 students were shortlisted for the OA (exact criteria is not known). Duration of the OA was 1.5 hours with no specific time allocated for a particular section. So one could switch between the sections. It was an audio and video proctored test conducted on the WeCP platform. This was a new platform for us and for some reason it was very sensitive to even minor movements. Almost everyone got flagged multiple times, sometimes just for a slight head tilt. This was stressful and one can easily fumble up in such situations. This was a common issue and there is nothing to be worried about even if it shows popups saying it will be included in the report. Section 1 - 2 Coding questions These were easy-moderate. I could solve them in around 20 minutes. If you have been consistent with your DSA practice you wouldn't have much problem here. 1) Find the maximum absolute difference between the sum of elements of any 2 non-empty subarrays of an array A of size N . Example - N=5 A = [5, -8, 2, -6, -9] In this case the two subarrays will be [5] and [-8,2,-6,-9] The absolute difference between the sum of their elements = 17 Solution - It is simple - find the maximum subarray sum and minimum subarray sum using Kadane’s algorithm. Max absolute difference = abs(max_sum - min_sum) 2) In each operation you can swap two adjacent characters of a string. Find minimum operations needed to reverse the string. Example - Input s = "bcd" Output 3 Here, operations would be - swap(1, 2) - "cbd" swap(2, 3) - "cdb" swap(1, 2) - "dcb" Solution - First create a reversed copy of the original string. Then, go through each position one by one and make sure that the character at that position matches the reversed version. For every character in the reversed string, we find where that same character currently is in the original string. If already correct then move on else bring it to the correct position by swapping it backward with its neighboring characters one at a time. Increment answer for every swap made. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/minimum-number-of-adjacent-swaps-to-reverse-a-string/ Section 2 - 16 MCQ questions The MCQs were a little tougher. They were based on CS fundamentals. Several DBMS questions were asked. Some niche SQL functions and OS questions were included. Time was definitely an important factor so choose wisely which ones to attempt properly. As long as your CS Fundamentals are clear, this should be fine. Section 3 - 3 video questions 20 sec to prepare + 1 min for answering Only 1 take (no retake) [ I had cleared JPMC’s hirevue round before this so I had a fair idea on how to approach them. You could definitely look up some common hirevue questions and get an idea.] Results - 20 people were shortlisted (+5 waitlisted ) for interviews which were on the next day itself. We received the results on 24th July, very late at night. So I would suggest not to waste time waiting and already start the interview preparation. Hilti usually holds OA and Interview on consecutive days hence I would advise starting interview preparation even before the OA so that you can be calm on the day before the interviews. Interviews Day - 25th July 2025 (OFFLINE) We were asked to report at 8.30 a.m. in college and interviews were scheduled to start from 9 a.m. onwards. We were supposed to dress in formal attire. I wore a white shirt with a black blazer over it, black formal trousers, and formal shoes. Dressing well is a must for interviews and it also helps with self confidence. There were 5 panels (each with 1 panelist) for conducting the technical interviews in parallel. Additionally 1 HR had accompanied them to conduct the HR round. The HR was also present in the Pre-Placement Talk. They conducted 1 Technical Round and then within 10-30 minutes informed whether one qualified for the HR Round or not. If yes, then we were escorted to the HR cabin room and immediately the HR Interview was conducted. Technical Round 1 - ( 45-50 minutes) I was the second in the list for my panel. While I was waiting for the person before me to complete his interview I had about 30 minutes. In this case, I would simply suggest avoiding last minute preparations. Re-iterate your introduction once in your mind before going in. I was called in at around 10 a.m. I greeted the interviewer with a smile and sat across. He mentioned that since he was a speaker during the Pre-Placement Talk I would know most things about him but still gave a brief introduction. He then asked me to introduce myself. I had memorized an introduction beforehand and had gotten it reviewed by my seniors during the mock interviews conducted by them. Introduction is a make or break and it is important to memorise it. Introduction tips - I would suggest keeping it precise and not more than 60-75 seconds. Your flow could be - 1) Name, branch etc 2) Technical aspects ( What domains you have worked on/are interested in, you can mention key projects, tech stack) 3) Achievements (if any) 4) Soft skills ( position in clubs, extra-curriculars, etc) 5) Hobbies ( keep this part less formal so that the intro ends on a light note with a smile on both faces) Additionally, as suggested by my seniors, you can introduce some breadcrumbs in your intro. These are like small, intentional cues that subtly guide them toward topics you want them to ask about. Maintain a good posture and eye contact, basically appear confident. He started the interview by asking me about what got me interested in the field of Computer Science. Then he moved to how my OA went. Apparently they had the results open on the screen. I didn't hesitate to mention the unnecessary flags everyone was getting and that it was scary. He wasn't aware of what all was asked in the OA so I gave him a quick rundown. He had no idea about the flagging and was surprised too. He then asked me to explain one of my projects. I talked about the first project on my resume which was a group project I did as a part of Project X. He confirmed whether it was a group project and I explained that we were a team of three and described my contribution. This led to a really good discussion. He asked whether I had chosen the group or not so I explained what project X is and how they conduct this whole mentorship programme with 2 rounds (proposal + interview) to select people. He seemed quite curious and interested in the whole process and asked several follow up questions that weren’t directly project related. We proceeded to talk about how I got comfortable working with people I didn't know, the roadblocks or disagreements we had and what role I played to resolve them. I also mentioned about the mentors involved, how they guided us throughout and how I was currently a mentor and doing the same thing for my juniors. He then proceeded to ask me about the second project in my resume. It was a RAG based project. He asked me what RAG is, why is it needed in general and why for my project. He also asked several other normal questions about my project. He was then glancing through my resume and saw python and c++ both mentioned in the tech stack, so he asked me about the difference between them and which one is used where. He then moved on to OOPS. I was asked to briefly explain all important concepts of OOPS ( basically 4 pillars, classes, objects). Then he questioned me about static vs dynamic polymorphism, the diamond problem in OOPS and how it is solved in c++ and a few other questions too. Surprisingly I was not asked any DBMS questions. Next he jumped on to DSA. I was asked only 1 question which was fairly simple. “Given a string of letters, find the maximum length of a block of consecutive identical letters and also identify which letter it is.” So if s = “bbccaaaappdddeeee” Answer is - a,4 ( This is because “aaaa” is the longest consecutive block with 4 a’s. There is also a consecutive block with 4 e’s but we want the first one) I started by explaining what came to my mind at first glance. I talked about storing the counts in a map while iterating through the string. While speaking, I realized there was no need for a map so I corrected myself with “Ok wait, we actually don’t even need a map here.” It’s important to correct yourself confidently. The solution was simply to iterate through the string while keeping a count and a maxCount variable and updating them accordingly. He then asked what to do if there are two blocks with the same maximum length. I asked whether we wanted the first or the last block. He said the first, so I explained that in that case we just don’t update maxCount when maxCount == count. After that he asked me to write the pseudocode on paper. Next came the puzzles. I was asked 2 puzzles. 1) https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/puzzle-set-35-2-eggs-and-100-floors/ 2) We have two water jugs, one measures 4 Gallons while the other measures 9 Gallons , how can we measure 6 gallons. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/puzzle-water-jug-problem/ I explained 2 approaches for the first one. He said I am on the right track but what if I want to further minimize it. I couldn't think of it at that time and he explained the solution to me. Sometimes the pressure does get you but explaining even non optimal approaches shows your thought process and that's equally important. I worked out the 2nd one on paper and got the solution fairly quickly. He finally asked me if I had any questions. I asked two questions. One of them was related to something he had mentioned during the Pre-Placement Talk. It shows that you paid attention and were genuinely interested and that’s something they appreciate. After that he said the interview was done and that I would be informed soon about whether I was moving to the next round or not. I thanked him and left the room. Around ten minutes later I was informed that I had been shortlisted for the HR Round and that it would happen immediately. I was asked to wait outside the HR cabin. A few tips for Technical Rounds - 1) When asked about something do not hesitate to ask follow up questions to clarify it. Sometimes they purposely leave out details and expect you to catch that. 2) There is no harm in mentioning that a project was a group project. In my case it actually led to a really engaging two way conversation. 3) Think everything aloud even if it sounds dumb. Firstly it's easier to realize you are on the wrong track if you are verbal about it and makes the interview less monotonous. Secondly, if you start drifting away from the right track the interviewer can guide you back. 4) If they ask you to write something, clarify whether you should explain as you write or write first and then then explain. Don’t start writing straight away. 5) Always prepare unique questions to ask them at the end. This is your chance to connect with them and show genuine interest in the firm. This is exactly where paying attention during the Pre-Placement Talk helps. HR Round - ( 15-20 minutes ) Around 12 students were shortlisted for the HR Round. Make sure you practice for this prior itself since you won't have much time between the two rounds. At around 12 p.m., I was called in for the HR round. She was the one who had started the Pre-Placement Talk so she didn't give her introduction by mentioning that we already know her. She began with “So keep aside your resume, I don't want to know what all is in there. Tell me anything that you want to.” This was a bit scary because you never know what they expect you to come up with on the spot. I answered it with “Ok, so I’ll start by sharing a few things about myself that aren’t on my resume.” One thing I’m genuinely proud of is the change I’ve gone through in college, so I took this opportunity to be raw and honest. Honesty never fails. This eventually led to me mentioning the key leadership roles I hold in the college committees and clubs. The conversation took a complete turn when I mentioned that I was appointed as the “Networking and Strategy Head of Project X”. She absolutely grilled me on it. It started with questions like “How will you keep the linkedin page updated? How frequently will you post stuff? Will you have that much content? Will that be sufficient? What if a post receives negative feedback?” What I mean is that it was like a rapid fire of questions. She kept interrupting me mid-answer, picking up on a few words from what I had just said and immediately launching into the next question. A couple of other questions on strategies to collaborate with other colleges were asked. The rapid fire finally ended with “Why do you think they appointed you for this position and if you were to appoint someone next year what would you look for? ”. She concluded by asking if I had any questions. I asked the two I had prepared and towards the end, I also shared some positive feedback I had heard from my seniors about Hilti’s work culture and environment. Mentioning these insights can leave a positive impression. I left the room quite surprised by the interview. There were no standard HR questions and nothing that I had prepared for. Still, I didn’t panic and I was pretty satisfied with my responses. I felt she was too. I’m fairly sure she was deliberately testing how I handled pressure and whether I could stay composed rather than panicking when bombarded with questions. Note - Everyone had a completely different HR Interview experience. Some were asked normal HR questions, some were asked about their resume projects, for some she didn't even look at the resume - so no one knew what to expect here. You must be ready for anything. Tips for HR Round - 1) If asked about future studies, say NO, even if you do have plans. It gives them a wrong opinion. 2) Prepare well for company based questions. They do test your interest in joining and knowledge about their work. 3) HR wants to understand who you are, not just what you know technically. Avoid mugged up answers. They are skilled at spotting rehearsed or fake answers. So speak naturally. 4) They can test you for pressure situations or your creativity by asking completely random questions. Communicate clearly and be calm and real with your responses. Results I was done with my interviews very early on and had to wait for around 4 hours. I was relaxed as the interviews were good from my end but obviously nervous for the results. We were asked to assemble in a room. I distinctly remember the tension building as we could see the panel having their final discussion through the glass window. They announced the results at around 5 p.m. 5 students were selected and luckily I was one of them! We all congratulated each other and I immediately called my parents to inform them of the good news. It felt like a huge weight had been lifted and all the preparation paid off ! Resources and Key Takeaways Resources 1.DSA - I had followed Striver's A2Z sheet and was 90% done with it by the time of interviews. (you can follow some other sheets too but be consistent) 2. OS, DBMS, CN, OOPS - OS and DBMS will usually be covered in your syllabus by the end of 2nd year. CN might not be covered. There are good youtube playlists like Gate Smashers. Also refer to GFG and InterviewBit for common interview questions. Some articles - OS, DBMS, OOPS . These are starters, you must try to understand important topics in depth. 3. System Design - There are resources available on YouTube. Try to understand both low and high level system design for specific cases like IRCTC, Uber, Zomato, etc. 4. HR - I didn't really look up answers for HR questions, I just noted down my own points for the common HR questions. I would suggest going through some sample answers but prepare your own. Give mock interviews It is extremely important to practice how you speak in an interview setting. Mocks conducted by your seniors in CoC is the best way to do that. If you aren't assigned any seniors for a mock, practice with your peers. Keep improving from the feedback and analyze your performance in the next mock. Do not procrastinate You have the whole 2 months of summer vacations with you to prepare for everything. Do enjoy your time but utilize it equally well . Trust me it will all be worth it when you get in! Start with OOPS, DBMS, CN, System Design at least a month before the drives start. This gives you enough time to revise and balance it with DSA prep to avoid last minute rushes. DSA and CS Fundamentals Select one sheet for DSA and follow that consistently. Try to come up with both brute and optimal approaches. Do not focus on the quantity of questions solved by comparing with peers. Knowing how to approach a question is one thing. Being able to explain it to someone from scratch is a completely different thing and equally important. So instead of trying to increase the count of your leetcode questions during the last 1-2 months, I would also suggest verbally practicing a few sums right from the brute force to the optimal approach. Trust me, take an easy to medium question - it will take you 5-10 minutes to solve but now try to explain it - you will struggle. For your CS fundamentals, I’d recommend mastering OOPS, DBMS, and OS first these are the core areas most companies focus on. After that, you can move on to System Design and Computer Networks (though CN isn’t asked very often). For OOPS in particular, make sure you also practice writing actual code, since many interviewers ask you to write on the spot. Once you feel confident with the fundamentals, go through the CoC archives and try answering previous interview questions out loud. Final Thoughts In my opinion, interviews are about 60% skill and communication and 40% luck. So don’t feel disheartened if you don’t clear an OA or if an interview doesn’t go the way you expected. A lot depends on the interviewer you get, their style of questioning and how they analyze. In fact, I received an offer from JPMC as well (after the CFG hackathon), a few weeks after getting into Hilti. I wasn’t sure how to process it at first, but I wasn’t disappointed either, because Hilti is an equally great company and I was genuinely happy with that opportunity. It just felt reassuring to know that my preparation had paid off in more than one place. What I mean is, some things really do come down to luck. You can’t control the timing but choosing to see things from a positive perspective makes all the difference. What you can control is your preparation. Be fully prepared from every angle, so that if you do face rejection, you can confidently tell yourself, “Maybe this one just wasn’t meant for me” instead of thinking “I should have prepared more.” There will be moments when people who seem less prepared land internships before you. Don't be disheartened, that’s how life works, isn't it? Once you get selected, celebrate and give yourself a well-deserved break. It’s an incredible feeling, something truly worth working for ! If you’ve got any questions or want advice related to internship preparation, feel free to reach out at ydmehta3115@gmail.com. It would be my pleasure to help out. ALL THE BEST ! YOU GOT THIS !
